blocks.text: A pathologist receives a colon biopsy slide in which one half of the section is dark, doubled over, and nuclei are unreadable. Before any diagnosis can be made, the first question is whether the problem lies in the patient's tissue or in how the slide was made.

blocks.markdown: Light passes through only thin, stable, contrasted specimens. Routine histology therefore converts soft, water-rich tissue into a wax-supported section a few micrometres thick: **fixation, dehydration, clearing, paraffin infiltration, embedding, sectioning, mounting and staining**. The aim is to keep structure close to the living state while making components visible by their chemistry.

blocks.title: Fixation
blocks.text: Fixation stabilises tissue so that autolysis (self-digestion by the cell's own enzymes) and bacterial decay stop and structure is held in place. Routine fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin (about 4% formaldehyde), which forms cross-links between proteins, mainly through amino groups, and so holds them in position. Fixative and timing vary by laboratory and purpose.

blocks.caption: Route from a biopsy to a stained paraffin section

Formalin cross-links proteins

Solvent such as xylene replaces alcohol
Alcohol does not mix with wax; solvent is miscible with both

Gives rigid support for cutting

blocks.title: Following a biopsy through the laboratory
blocks.prompt: A 3 mm skin punch biopsy arrives in formalin. List the steps needed before it can be viewed.

steps.text: It is fixed in formalin so that proteins are cross-linked and autolysis stops.
It is dehydrated in graded alcohols and cleared in xylene because paraffin cannot enter water-containing tissue.
Molten paraffin infiltrates and the tissue is embedded in a block.
A microtome cuts sections about 4-5 micrometres thick, which are floated flat and picked up on a slide.
The wax is removed, the section rehydrated, stained with H&E and coverslipped.

blocks.answer: Fixation, dehydration, clearing, infiltration, embedding, sectioning, staining, mounting.

blocks.markdown: **Why H&E colours tissue.** Haematoxylin is oxidised to haematein and combined with an aluminium salt (a **mordant**), forming a positively charged complex. This complex binds negatively charged groups, mainly the phosphate groups of DNA and RNA, so nuclei (and RNA-rich cytoplasm such as that of plasma cells, where abundant rough ER is present, and sulfated proteoglycans of cartilage matrix) stain blue-purple: they are **basophilic**. **Eosin** is a negatively charged (anionic) dye used at acidic pH, where many proteins carry positive charge on lysine and arginine side chains, so it stains cytoplasmic proteins, collagen and haemoglobin pink: they are **eosinophilic**.

blocks.title: Basophilic versus eosinophilic
blocks.text: Basophilic = binds the basic (positively charged) haematoxylin complex, so the tissue component is acidic or anionic (nucleic acids, sulfated glycosaminoglycans). Eosinophilic = binds the acidic (negatively charged) eosin, so the component is basic or cationic (many proteins).

blocks.title: Predicting H&E colour
blocks.prompt: A section contains a plasma cell, a bundle of collagen and an erythrocyte. Predict the colour of each.

steps.text: The plasma cell nucleus is blue-purple; its cytoplasm is also purple-blue because abundant rough ER is rich in RNA.
Collagen is a protein-rich matrix that binds eosin and stains pink.
The erythrocyte is full of haemoglobin, a protein, so it stains bright pink-red.

blocks.answer: Plasma cell blue-purple, collagen pink, erythrocyte pink-red.

blocks.markdown: **Quantifying shrinkage.** Percentage shrinkage equals $(L_{\text{before}} - L_{\text{after}})/L_{\text{before}} \times 100$. Serial sectioning also lets you plan depth: the number of sections needed to cut through a thickness $d$ at section thickness $t$ is about $d/t$.

items: Fixation first, then dehydration, clearing, infiltration, embedding, sectioning, staining.
Haematoxylin (with a mordant) stains acidic components blue-purple; eosin stains basic proteins pink.
Always check for folds, shrinkage, tears and chatter before interpreting a slide.

blocks.title: Common interpretation pitfall
blocks.text: Do not diagnose a cleft, a dark band or a missing strip as disease until you have asked whether it is an artefact of processing or cutting.

points: Routine preparation runs fixation, dehydration, clearing, paraffin infiltration, embedding, sectioning, mounting and H&E staining, each step solving a specific problem.
Haematoxylin plus mordant binds anionic nucleic acids and stains them blue-purple; eosin binds cationic proteins and stains them pink.
Folds, shrinkage clefts, tears and chatter are artefacts that must be recognised before interpretation.

questions.stem: A technician places a formalin-fixed kidney specimen directly into molten paraffin. The block cuts poorly and the sections crumble with patchy, unstained holes. Which omitted steps explain this?

options.text: Dehydration and clearing, because paraffin cannot infiltrate water-containing tissue
Fixation, because formalin is needed for paraffin to melt
Staining, because dyes help wax set
Mounting, because coverslips support the wax

questions.correctOptionText: Dehydration and clearing, because paraffin cannot infiltrate water-containing tissue

distractorRationale.d: Mounting occurs after sectioning and does not affect infiltration.

questions.explanation: Paraffin is hydrophobic and cannot enter tissue that still contains water. Dehydration in alcohols and clearing in a solvent miscible with wax are needed first.

questions.stem: A laboratory accidentally prepares haematoxylin without its aluminium salt and nuclei stain very weakly. What is the role of the aluminium salt?

options.text: It acts as a mordant, forming a positively charged complex that binds nucleic acid phosphate groups
It cross-links proteins as formalin does
It makes eosin positively charged
It dissolves the wax from the section

questions.correctOptionText: It acts as a mordant, forming a positively charged complex that binds nucleic acid phosphate groups

distractorRationale.b: Cross-linking is the job of the fixative.
distractorRationale.d: Wax is removed with a solvent such as xylene.

questions.explanation: Haematein alone binds poorly; with aluminium it forms a cationic complex that binds the negatively charged phosphates of DNA and RNA. Nuclei are therefore blue-purple.

questions.stem: A section of tumour shows clear clefts around every nest of cells, with no matching change in the patient's imaging. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Shrinkage artefact from fixation and dehydration
A tear from a blunt microtome blade
A fold from poor flattening
Chatter from vibration

questions.correctOptionText: Shrinkage artefact from fixation and dehydration
questions.explanation: Retraction clefts around cell groups are a classic shrinkage artefact because tissue volume changes during processing. A fold, tear or chatter would look different.

questions.stem: In life an artery was measured at 300 micrometres across on a fresh-frozen reference section; on the processed paraffin slide it measures 255 micrometres. Calculate the percentage shrinkage from processing.
questions.explanation: Shrinkage = (300 - 255) / 300 x 100 = 15%. A shrinkage of this size shows why dimensions measured on stained sections must be interpreted with caution.

questions.stem: Explain why fixation, dehydration and clearing are each needed before a tissue can be cut as a paraffin section.
markingGuide: Fixation (e.g. formalin) cross-links proteins and stops autolysis and decay.
Dehydration in graded alcohols removes water because paraffin and water do not mix; graded steps limit distortion.
Clearing replaces alcohol with a solvent (e.g. xylene) miscible with both alcohol and wax.
Paraffin then infiltrates and supports the tissue for microtome sectioning.
questions.explanation: Each step removes an obstacle for the next: fixation preserves, dehydration removes water, clearing bridges alcohol to wax.

questions.stem: A section shows fine parallel bands of alternating thick and thin tissue at regular intervals across its whole width. Which artefact and cause fit?

options.text: Chatter, from blade vibration or a blunt blade
Fold, from poor flattening on the water bath
Shrinkage, from poor dehydration
Tear, from a hard tissue inclusion

questions.correctOptionText: Chatter, from blade vibration or a blunt blade

distractorRationale.b: A fold is one doubled dark region.
distractorRationale.d: A tear is a single linear break.

questions.explanation: Regular parallel ripples are characteristic of chatter. They can mimic structural striations and reduce clarity.

questions.stem: A pathologist wants to examine a lesion lying 0.5 mm deeper in the block. Sections are cut at 4 micrometres. How many sections must be cut to reach 0.5 mm?
questions.explanation: 0.5 mm is 500 micrometres, and 500 / 4 = 125 sections of 4 micrometres. Such arithmetic shows how thin routine sections are.

questions.stem: On H&E, the cytoplasm of a cell in a bone marrow smear section is deep purple-blue instead of pink, and it has an eccentric nucleus with a perinuclear pale zone. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Abundant RNA in rough ER makes the cytoplasm basophilic, as in a plasma cell
Abundant haemoglobin makes the cytoplasm basophilic
Abundant collagen makes the cytoplasm basophilic
Eosin has failed to enter the nucleus

questions.correctOptionText: Abundant RNA in rough ER makes the cytoplasm basophilic, as in a plasma cell

distractorRationale.d: This does not explain cytoplasmic colour.

questions.explanation: RNA phosphate groups bind the cationic haematoxylin complex, so RNA-rich cytoplasm appears blue-purple. A plasma cell with a large rough ER secreting antibody is a classic example.

questions.stem: Distinguish a fold, a tear and shrinkage on a slide by appearance and cause, and explain why recognising them matters before reporting.
markingGuide: Fold: dark doubled region from poor flattening; obscures nuclei.
Tear: sharp linear break or missing strip from hard tissue, damaged knife or poor cutting.
Shrinkage: clefts or spaces around cells from volume change during processing.
Recognition prevents mistaking artefacts for true pathology.
questions.explanation: Each artefact has a distinct appearance and origin. Misreading them as disease can lead to wrong conclusions.

questions.stem: Cartilage matrix rich in sulfated glycosaminoglycans stains blue-purple on H&E. How is it described?

options.text: Basophilic, because its anionic groups bind the cationic haematoxylin complex
Eosinophilic, because it binds eosin
Acidophilic, because it is basic
Unstained, because H&E cannot stain matrix

questions.correctOptionText: Basophilic, because its anionic groups bind the cationic haematoxylin complex

distractorRationale.c: Acidophilic means eosinophilic and the matrix is anionic.

questions.explanation: Sulfate and carboxyl groups carry negative charge, so they bind the positively charged haematoxylin complex. Any strongly acidic component can be basophilic, not only nuclei.
